subject: anaesthesia
title: Mechanical Ventilation: Modes, Lung-Protective Strategy, and Weaning Indices

steps.title: Volume Control versus Pressure Control
steps.tx: **Volume control and pressure control ventilation mechanics** contrast fundamental delivery algorithms: Volume Control Ventilation (VCV) guarantees a preset tidal volume (VT) regardless of changing lung compliance, delivering gas with a constant square-wave inspiratory flow that results in variable peak airway pressures. In contrast, Pressure Control Ventilation (PCV) guarantees a preset inspiratory pressure with a decelerating flow pattern, resulting in variable tidal volumes.

In contrast, Pressure Control Ventilation (PCV) guarantees a preset inspiratory pressure with a decelerating flow pattern, resulting in variable tidal volumes.

steps.tx: Two waveform pairs on this ventilator screen describe opposite promises. Volume control delivers its set breath with a square flow pattern and lets pressure fall where compliance dictates, while pressure control caps the pressure and lets volume wander. Reading the **pressure and flow scalars** together tells you which promise your patient is actually receiving and how stiff lungs are rewriting it breath by breath. A climbing pressure trace at constant flow warns of worsening compliance long before an alarm bothers to sound.
steps.say: Comparing pressure and flow scalars distinguishes volume control from pressure control ventilation at the bedside.

steps.title: Decelerating Flow in Pressure Control
steps.tx: **Decelerating flow profile of pressure control** delivers maximum inspiratory gas flow at the start of inspiration when lung volume is lowest and airway resistance is easily overcome, tapering down as alveolar pressure approaches target peak pressure. This decelerating flow pattern achieves lower peak airway pressures, optimizes alveolar recruitment in stiff non-compliant lung units, and improves gas distribution in acute respiratory distress syndrome.

steps.title: Lung-Protective ARDS Ventilation
steps.tx: **ARDS Network lung-protective ventilation protocol** minimizes ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma and barotrauma) through three strict parameters: low tidal volumes of 4 to 8 milliliters per kilogram of predicted body weight (PBW, calculated from patient height and sex, never actual weight), maintaining end-inspiratory plateau pressure (P-plat) strictly under 30 cmH2O, and applying positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).

rows: Reduce tidal volume down to 4 mL/kg if P-plat high

Accepts respiratory acidosis to protect lungs

steps.tx: This protocol shrinks the breath to protect the lung from its own ventilator. Tidal volumes of six millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight, plateau pressure held below thirty, and PEEP titrated by table make up the **ARDS Network protocol** that first proved gentleness saves lives in ARDS. Predicted weight comes from height and sex, never the scales, a detail whose neglect quietly volutraumatises obese patients. The schematic's discipline feels restrictive until you remember the alternative stretches injured alveoli like overblown balloons.
steps.say: Low tidal volume by predicted weight with plateau pressure limits is the lung protective ARDS Network strategy.

steps.title: PEEP and Alveolar Derecruitment
steps.tx: **Positive end-expiratory pressure mechanisms** prevent end-expiratory alveolar collapse (atelectasis) and cyclic recruitment-derecruitment shear stress (atelectotrauma). By maintaining positive airway pressure at end-expiration, PEEP increases functional residual capacity, shifts tidal ventilation onto the compliant linear portion of the respiratory pressure-volume curve, and redistributes extravascular lung water, reducing intrapulmonary shunt fraction.

steps.title: Peak versus Plateau Pressures
steps.tx: **Peak inspiratory and plateau pressure differentiation** isolates resistive airway pathology from compliance elastance pathology: Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP) reflects total resistance of the ventilator circuit, endotracheal tube, and airways plus lung compliance. Plateau pressure (measured during an end-inspiratory pause) reflects pure static compliance of the respiratory system (lung parenchyma plus chest wall).

steps.title: Ventilator Weaning and RSBI
steps.tx: **Rapid shallow breathing index weaning predictor** (Tobin RSBI) is calculated during one minute of unassisted spontaneous breathing via a T-piece or minimal pressure support: RSBI equals respiratory frequency (f in breaths/min) divided by tidal volume (VT in liters). An RSBI under 105 breaths/min/L strongly predicts successful extubation, whereas an RSBI exceeding 105 indicates impending diaphragmatic exhaustion and weaning failure.

steps.title: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) Bundle
steps.tx: **Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle** slashes secondary nosocomial lung infections in mechanically ventilated patients through evidence-based nursing and clinical interventions: maintain head-of-bed elevation strictly between 30 and 45 degrees (preventing passive aspiration of gastric contents), daily sedation vacations with spontaneous breathing trials, continuous subglottic secretion drainage, and avoidance of routine ventilator circuit changes.

steps.title: Arterial Blood Gas Systematic Analysis
steps.tx: **Systematic arterial blood gas interpretation** follows a five-step diagnostic framework: evaluate pH (normal 7.35 to 7.45; acidosis under 7.35, alkalosis over 7.45), assess primary respiratory driver via PaCO2 (normal 35 to 45 mmHg), assess metabolic component via serum bicarbonate (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), calculate the anion gap (Na minus [Cl plus HCO3]; normal 8 to 12 mEq/L) to distinguish high-anion gap from normal-anion gap acidosis, and evaluate oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ratio).
